who: Duane J. Osheim, historian of medieval and Renaissance Italy at the University of Virginia; PhD UC Davis, 1973.

evidence.says: The Daily Progress obituary identifies Duane Jeffrey Osheim as a historian of medieval and early Renaissance Italy, with a UC Davis PhD in 1973, hired by the UVA history department in 1976.
The authority for Duane J. Osheim cites An Italian ... (1977), whose preliminary pages identify his PhD institution as the University of California, Davis.
The item identifies Duane J. Osheim and links LC authority n77019601.

notes: Full name, doctorate institution and year, historical field, and UVA career agree with the supervisor record.

who: Marline Otte, historian of modern Europe and German cultural history at Tulane; PhD Toronto, 1999.

evidence.says: Tulane identifies Otte as an associate professor specializing in modern European and German cultural history, with a Toronto PhD in 1999.
Tulane lists Otte as advisor of Helma Kaldewey (2014) and chair of Catherine Wilkins’s dissertation committee (2008), with the titles in the supplied records.
The authority cites Otte’s 1999 Toronto history PhD thesis and the 2006 book Jewish Identities in German Popular Entertainment, also listed on her Tulane page.

notes: Both supplied students are explicitly linked to Otte by the department; the candidate’s authority record and doctorate agree.

who: Doug (Douglas) Owram, historian of Canada, formerly University of Alberta history faculty; PhD Toronto.

evidence.says: UBC identifies Doug Owram as a historian who completed his PhD at Toronto, joined Alberta’s history department in 1976, became professor in 1985, and served as vice-president from 1995 to 2003.
LC records Douglas Owram as a variant of Doug Owram; Promise of Eden identifies him with Alberta’s history department, and A History of the Canadian Economy uses Douglas Owram.
The item identifies Doug Owram as a historian and academic administrator and links LC n80088757.

notes: The authority explicitly joins the Doug and Douglas forms. Institution, field and doctorate institution agree; later student completion dates do not require a different person.

who: Max Page, historian of cities and architecture at UMass Amherst; PhD in history, Pennsylvania, 1995.

evidence.says: Page’s institutional CV records a history PhD from Pennsylvania in 1995 and teaching at UMass Amherst from 2001 onward.
UMass identifies Page as a professor who writes about the history of cities and architecture and lists his Pennsylvania PhD, 1995.
The authority for Max Page describes him as professor of architecture and history at UMass Amherst and author of The Creative Destruction of Manhattan and The City’s End.

notes: The LC candidate has the correct institution and works; the institutional CV independently confirms the exact doctorate and employment during both students’ degrees.

who: Edward Pessen, historian of the nineteenth-century United States at Baruch and the CUNY Graduate Center; PhD Columbia, 1954.

evidence.says: LC identifies Edward Pessen, author of The Social Philosophies of Early American Leaders of Labor, and explicitly records his Columbia PhD, 1954.
The AHA’s 1970 program identifies the author of Jacksonian America as Edward Pessen of the CUNY Graduate Center.
The 1984–85 Fulbright directory identifies Edward Pessen as distinguished professor of history at Baruch College and the CUNY Graduate Center, specializing in U.S. history, 1789–1865.

notes: The candidate’s exact doctorate matches; contemporary sources place the historian at the students’ graduate institution around their degree years.

who: Ulrich Bonnell Phillips, historian of the antebellum South at Michigan and Yale; PhD Columbia, 1902.

evidence.says: The Georgia Historical Society records Phillips’s Columbia PhD in 1902, Michigan teaching in 1911–29 and Yale teaching in 1929–34.
Yale identifies U. B. Phillips with the Ulrich Bonnell Phillips Papers and confirms that he taught at Yale from 1929 to 1934.
LC identifies Ulrich Bonnell Phillips as the author of Georgia and State Rights (1902) and a University of Michigan history professor.

notes: The name, doctorate and successive institutions match. Glunt’s 1931 completion followed Phillips’s move from Michigan to Yale; the completion date alone does not contradict prior supervision.

who: George Wilson Pierson, Yale historian and Larned Professor of History; PhD Yale, 1933.

evidence.says: Yale’s finding aid for the George Wilson Pierson Papers records his Yale PhD in 1933 and his appointment as Larned Professor of History from 1946 to 1973.
LC identifies George Wilson Pierson, with George W. Pierson and G. W. Pierson as usages, and cites Tocqueville and Beaumont in America (1938).
The item identifies George Wilson Pierson as a historian, lists Yale as employer, and links LC n50016851.

notes: The exact doctorate and Yale professorship covering both 1968 and 1971 identify the candidate as the supervisor.

who: John R. Porter, historian of Quebec art and professor at Université Laval; doctorate Montréal, 1981.

evidence.says: The official biography identifies John R. Porter as an art historian, records his Montréal doctorate in 1981, and describes his teaching at Laval, including doctoral students and continuing associate-professor status in 2004.
The John R. Porter candidate is the author of Studies in Euripides’ Orestes, an assistant professor at Saskatchewan, with a Toronto PhD in 1990.
This authority identifies J. M. Porter as Jene M. Porter, author of Sophia and Praxis.
The scholarly society program identifies Jene M. Porter with the University of Saskatchewan and work in political theory.
The John Porter item linked to LC n98075676 identifies a sociologist associated with Carleton, rather than the Laval art historian.

notes: None of the three candidates matches the Laval art historian. The Toronto doctorate in the supplied own_phd field conflicts with his Montréal doctorate and appears to conflate him with the Saskatchewan classicist; do not merge on that fact.
